title: Family Finds Chicken in Veg Biryani at Bengaluru Airport, Probe Begins
excerpt: A strictly vegetarian family from Varanasi says small pieces of chicken were mixed into a veg biryani billed as vegetarian at a Terminal 1 eatery; the airport operator and the outlet's operator say they are investigating, while food safety authorities have not commented.
body:
• A family from Varanasi travelling through Bengaluru airport's Terminal 1 says it found small pieces of chicken in a veg biryani ordered at Taste of India, near gates 16 and 17, and that children had already eaten some of it.
  • Piyush Agrawal, who posted videos of the confrontation on X on October 31, 2026, says the bill listed the dish as veg biryani and that the manager and chef confirmed chicken was in the food.
  • Airport operator Bangalore International Airport Ltd said it is investigating and cannot comment until the probe is complete; HMSHost Services India, which operates the outlet, confirmed meat was found but said the cause was not yet established.
  • The family has asked the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and airport authorities to check CCTV footage and order records; the food safety authorities have not commented in the reporting so far.

What the family says happened

According to reporting by The Times of India, the family was travelling from Bengaluru to Varanasi when it stopped at Taste of India in Terminal 1 of Kempegowda International Airport. The group ordered a vegetarian biryani to share before boarding. After a few bites, they noticed small pieces of what appeared to be chicken mixed into the rice, the reports say.

In videos posted on X, a woman from the group holds up the plate showing small bits of meat among the grains of rice. Agrawal, recording the dish, says: "Look, we ordered veg biryani, and found tiny pieces of chicken in this." He later clarified that he did not receive a fully non-vegetarian biryani, but that it contained small bits of chicken.

The family says it is strictly vegetarian and that the discovery caused severe distress and hurt religious sentiments, particularly because children had unknowingly eaten some of the food before the pieces were noticed. Agrawal also said the family was still asked to pay the full bill and was not given a refund.

The confrontation and the response

Airport security and floor staff stepped in and urged the restaurant to bring out the manager and kitchen staff to explain how non-vegetarian food reached a vegetarian order, according to the reporting. The family says the manager and chef eventually acknowledged that chicken was present.

"We are treating the matter with utmost seriousness and are conducting a thorough internal review to establish the facts and circumstances."

— Kathhiravan Radhakrishnan, Director of Operations, HMSHost Services India

Soon after the videos circulated, airport operator Bangalore International Airport Ltd (BIAL) acknowledged the incident. An official told The Times of India: "We are investigating the matter and cannot say anything until the probe is complete."

Kathhiravan Radhakrishnan, director of operations at HMSHost Services India Pvt Ltd, which operates the restaurant, said the matter was of grave concern and that he understood the distress it caused. He confirmed that meat was found in the dish but said the reason for the mishap was yet to be ascertained, The Times of India reported. The outlet also said it was conducting a thorough internal review.

What happens next

The family has asked the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and Bengaluru airport authorities to investigate urgently, check CCTV footage and order records, and take strict action if a breach is established. It says it has kept the bill and the food as evidence.

The Times of India also approached FSSAI and the Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration, but neither offered comments on the matter, according to the reporting. That means, for now, the key unresolved question is how the meat got into the dish — whether it was a labelling error, a serving mix-up, or cross-contamination in the kitchen. The internal review and any regulator action will have to establish that; no finding has been reported yet.

Why this has resonated

For many vegetarian travellers, the incident touches a point of trust: a dish labelled vegetarian on a bill is taken at face value, especially at an airport where passengers eat quickly between flights. Online reaction split between sympathy for the family and debate about the risks of eating at outlets that serve both vegetarian and non-vegetarian food. The counter-argument from most commenters, as reported, was straightforward: if a counter lists a vegetarian option and charges for it, keeping meat out of that dish is the minimum requirement, not an extra precaution the customer must police.

Until the investigation reports, the story stands as an allegation backed by video, a bill the family says listed the dish as vegetarian, and an operator confirmation that meat was found — with the cause still open. Travellers with strict dietary requirements may want to confirm an order verbally at mixed-menu outlets and keep the receipt, as this family did, so any complaint can be traced to a specific order.
nri_angle: Vegetarian diaspora travellers passing through Indian airports face the same labelling and cross-contamination risk this family says it encountered at Bengaluru airport.
author: Diaspora Desk
